title: Post-incident review: checkout outage
scenario: Meeting transcript: a five-person post-incident review with three explicit agreements, two proposals that were not agreed (one disputed), action items with and without deadlines, open questions, a repeated timeline and small talk.
audience: The payments and support teams, and anyone who missed the review
objective: Know exactly what was agreed, what was only proposed, who owes what by when, and what is still unknown, without the canvas inventing agreement or dates.

units.quote: Attendees: Dana (facilitator), Marcus (on-call SRE), Leila (payments backend lead), Tomás (release engineering), Kenji (customer support lead)

omittable.note: Attendee list; names reappear with what each person said and owns.

units.quote: Dana: Okay, I think everyone's here. Did people manage to grab coffee? The machine on four is broken again.
Kenji: I brought my own. Lesson learned.
Dana: Smart. Right, let's start.
This is the blameless review for the checkout outage on Friday, March 14.
Marcus, can you walk us through the timeline?
At 16:40 a config change to the payments service went out.
It changed the gateway connection pool from 50 connections to 5.
That was a typo; the intent was 55.
Checkout requests started queuing for a connection and timing out almost immediately.
Our error-rate alert fired at 17:02, so 22 minutes after the change.
I rolled the config back at 17:15, and checkout was fully recovered at 17:27.
So customers saw errors for 47 minutes in total.
And on our side, we counted about 2,300 failed checkouts in that window.
Support got 140 tickets before we posted the status page.
Dana: Why did the alert take 22 minutes?

omittable.note: A question answered in the next turn.

units.quote: The alert only fires when the checkout error rate is above 10% for 15 minutes.
Errors went over 10% around 16:47, so the earliest it could fire was 17:02.
It did exactly what it was configured to do.
Leila: Which is too slow for checkout.
15 minutes of sustained errors is a long time when every minute is lost revenue.
Dana: Fair. What do we want instead?
I'd propose 5% over 5 minutes for checkout specifically.
I checked the last 30 days and that would have paged twice on noise, both during the payment provider's own maintenance.
Leila: Two noisy pages a month is fine for checkout.
Dana: Anyone against? ... Okay.
Agreed: we'll lower the checkout error-rate alert to 5% over 5 minutes.
Marcus, can you own that?
Marcus: Yes. I'll have it changed by Wednesday, March 19.
Kenji: One more thing from support.
The status page went up at 17:20, which is 40 minutes after the errors started.
Customers were asking on social media before we said anything.
Dana: Who posts the status page today?

omittable.note: A question answered in the next turn.

units.quote: Kenji: Whoever is incident commander, when they remember. On Friday that was Marcus, and he was busy rolling back.
Marcus: Honestly, it was the last thing on my mind.
Dana: Should support be allowed to post it directly?
Kenji: I'd like that, yes.
Leila: No objection from me.
Dana: Agreed: support can post a status-page update directly, without waiting for the incident commander.

critical.note: Agreed decision 2; no owner or date was given.

units.quote: Dana: Great. Next, how did a config value like that get through?
Leila: Config changes don't go through code review.
They're edited in the deploy dashboard and applied directly.
Code changes need two approvals; config needs none.
Tomás: That's the real gap. A typo in code would have been caught by the reviewer or by a test.
Dana: So the proposal is that payments config goes through the same review as code?
Leila: Yes. Config lives in the repo, it gets a pull request, and it needs one approval from the payments team.
Tomás: I'm fine with that.
Marcus: Same.
Agreed: config changes to the payments service will go through pull-request review with one payments-team approval.
Leila, can you set that up?
Leila: I'll move the config into the repo and add the approval rule by Friday, March 21.
Tomás: Can I raise something else?
I'd like us to stop deploying anything to payments after 15:00 on Fridays.

critical.note: A proposal that was disputed and not agreed.

units.quote: This went out at 16:40 on a Friday, and half the team had already logged off.
Leila: I don't agree with that.

critical.note: The objection that leaves the freeze unagreed.

units.quote: A freeze just moves the risk to Monday morning, when traffic is higher.
The problem here wasn't the day, it was that nobody reviewed the change.
Tomás: The review fixes this one cause. But fewer people around means slower recovery for any cause.
Leila: Recovery took 25 minutes after the alert, and Marcus was on call. Being Friday didn't slow that down.
Tomás: That's one incident. I think we'd see a pattern if we looked.
Dana: I don't think we're going to settle this today.
Let's not decide the freeze now.
Tomás, could you pull the incidents from the last six months and see whether late-Friday deploys are over-represented?
Bring it to the next review on April 2.

critical.note: Owner Tomás, due at the review on April 2.

units.quote: Tomás: Sure, I can do that.
Marcus: While we're on prevention, I'd also propose automatic rollback: if the checkout error rate doubles within 10 minutes of a deploy, the pipeline rolls back on its own.

critical.note: A proposal with an unresolved objection.

units.quote: Leila: For config, maybe. For code, I'm nervous.
If a release includes a database migration, rolling back the code without the migration can leave us worse off.
Marcus: We could exclude releases with migrations.
Leila: Possibly. I'd want to know how often we ship migrations before I agree to anything.
Dana: Okay, so auto-rollback is an open question.
We don't know how many releases include migrations.
Let's leave it open.
Kenji: Can I go back to customers?
Do we know whether any of the 2,300 failed checkouts were retried successfully?

critical.note: Unanswered; it shapes the customer email.

units.quote: If most people retried, the email we send is different.
Marcus: I don't know. The payment logs would show it, but nobody has looked yet.
Dana: That's an open question too, then.
Kenji, can you draft the customer email either way?
Kenji: Yes, I'll take the email draft.

critical.note: Owner Kenji; no deadline was stated, and none may be invented.

units.quote: Marcus: So just to recap the timeline again for the doc: the change went out at 16:40, the alert fired at 17:02, rollback at 17:15, recovered at 17:27.

omittable.note: Repeats the timeline of u7, u11 and u12.

units.quote: Dana: Thanks. Anything else? ... Okay. Good review, everyone. And someone please report the coffee machine.

safeToOmit.why: Small talk about coffee and sign-offs.
The timeline repeated for the notes; it adds nothing to u7, u11 and u12.

provenance.note: Original transcript written for this dataset. The people (Dana, Marcus, Leila, Tomás, Kenji), the outage, all times, counts and dates are invented.
